hints: Start by thinking where insect resistance comes from in nature - which bacterium makes a protein toxic to insects, and so what DNA must be taken?
Recall the standard tools for cutting DNA and making many copies of a wanted gene before it can be used.
Think about what carrier is needed to hold the gene and what control sequence must be added so maize cells will switch it on.
Remember the enzyme that joins DNA pieces together to make recombinant DNA.
Finish by thinking how the recombinant DNA gets into maize cells and what the grown plant must then do to show resistance.
walkthrough:
Get the Bt resistance gene**
The resistance is not invented, it is borrowed. The soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis has a gene coding for Bt toxin protein that kills insects. You cut that gene out of bacterial DNA with a restriction enzyme, also called an endonuclease, and then make many copies by PCR so you have enough to work with.

Build recombinant DNA**
You need a vector to carry the gene. The Bt gene is inserted into a plasmid, with a promoter added in front so the maize cell will transcribe it. DNA ligase then seals the sugar-phosphate backbone to form complete recombinant DNA. In plants this is often done using the Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens.

Put it into maize and grow resistant plants**
The recombinant plasmid is taken up by maize tissue, cells, callus or embryos. Those transformed cells are grown into whole plants. Because the Bt gene is now part of their DNA, they express it and produce Bt toxin in their tissues, so feeding insects are killed.

Final answer: Isolate Bt toxin gene/DNA from Bacillus thuringiensis using restriction endonuclease; amplify by PCR; insert into plasmid vector with promoter and seal with DNA ligase; transfer recombinant plasmid into maize tissue/cells/embryo e.g. using Agrobacterium tumefaciens Ti plasmid; maize expresses gene and produces Bt toxin.

hints: Compare the three bars at each time point - look at white and light grey bars versus the dark grey bar on days 2, 3 and 4.
Look along the time axis for the dark grey bars only - what happens to survival as days of feeding increase from 1 to 4?
walkthrough:
Separate the effect of pollen from the effect of Bt**
White bars, no pollen, and light grey bars, non-Bt pollen, both stay at about 100% survival on days 1 to 4. That tells you plain pollen and leaves are not harmful. Only the dark grey bars, Bt pollen, fall - to about 87% on day 2, about 67% on day 3 and about 55% on day 4.

Link time to dose**
So the conclusion is that Bt toxin in pollen is toxic to monarch caterpillars, and the effect is cumulative. More days eating Bt pollen means lower percentage survival.

Final answer: Pollen from Bt maize kills/harms caterpillars while pollen from non-Bt maize and leaves with no pollen do not; longer feeding on Bt pollen causes greater fall in survival, e.g. ~87% at day 2 to ~55% at day 4.

hints: Think about exposure in the field - for harm to happen, Bt pollen must actually land on milkweed leaves that caterpillars eat.
Think about where and when - are maize fields and milkweeds always side by side, and is pollen shed exactly when caterpillars feed?
Think about what happens to insect populations over 20 years of exposure to a toxin.
Think about how a laboratory dusting of leaves might differ from wind dispersal in amount and toxicity.
walkthrough:
No exposure means no effect**
In the lab every caterpillar was forced to eat leaves heavily dusted with Bt pollen. In nature, wind may carry most Bt pollen away so little deposits on milkweeds. Milkweeds may also grow in different areas from maize fields, so many caterpillars never meet Bt pollen.

Timing and biology reduce risk**
Even where they overlap, maize may shed pollen at a different time from when caterpillars are actively feeding, so exposure is brief. Over 20 years from 1999 to 2019, caterpillars could also develop resistance to Bt toxin by natural selection, and lab pollen quantity or toxicity may have been artificially high compared with field pollen.

Other ecological factors dominate**
Monarch numbers are affected by many variables such as weather, breeding conditions and herbicide use reducing milkweed. Better conditions in 2019 could increase counts and mask any small Bt effect, so the lab prediction does not transfer directly to the real ecosystem.

Final answer: Any four: Bt pollen may not deposit on milkweed in field / is diluted by wind; caterpillars and Bt maize in different areas; pollen shed at different time to caterpillar feeding; caterpillars evolved resistance to Bt toxin; lab dose/quantity/toxicity higher than field; other field factors e.g. better breeding conditions in 2019.
